content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
On its surface structure, the paper looks well organized and existing literature on disentangled representations is well reviewed. However, the paper is extremely difficult to read and it is hard to follow the reasoning of the authors. I hope that the authors can clarify misunderstandings during rebuttal.

“Existing works on disentangled representation learning usually lie on a common assumption: all factors in a disentangled representation should be independent. We argue that this assumption is not sufficient and another assumption is vital for disentangled representation learning: information contained in each factor of a disentangled representation is irrelevant to others, i.e. the containing information about data of factors is isolated. “

-How can the first sentence be claimed if there is not a consensus about the formal definition of disentangled representations as stated in the introduction?
- Assuming that ‘.. [Independence] is not sufficient  for disentangled representation learning’. Then you propose an additional assumption that seems to be the central contribution of the present paper:

‘information contained in each factor of a disentangled representation is irrelevant to others, i.e. the containing information about data of factors is isolated’.

- I don’t understand this notion of information that must be different than independence, namely that ‘information contained in each factor [...] is irrelevant to other [factors] ’ and 
‘the containing information about data of factors is isolated’.

I guess the notions of ‘data of factors’, and ‘information being isolated’, ‘irrelevant information’ need to be clarified. The text in the introduction is unfortunately also not very helpful

“... Since each factor [...] corresponds to a single factor of variation in data, 
each factor only contains the information of the corresponding factor of variation in data.”

I think there is a collection of ‘factors’ and a collection of ‘factors of variation in data’, and between these two objects there is a correspondence. The statement ‘each factor only contains the information of the corresponding factor of variation in data’ implies that a ‘factor of variation in data’ is an object that posses information that is contained in the factor.
				
At the end of the introduction, the authors state 
‘conditional independence originates from no-sharing-parameter block and the independence’ of noise in reparameterization trick, which can be regarded as inductive biases on model. 

This statement is alarming as it hints at a clash of terminology, the concept of independence in the information theoretic/probabilistic sense -- that is the density of two random variables can be written exactly as the product of marginals -- with ‘the lack of a functional dependence’. 
(Consider the Box-Muller method for generating independent Gaussian random variables x and y, where x = r cos(2pi u) and y = r sin(2 pi u) where u is uniform on the unit interval and r is exponential with rate 2. x and y are independent random variables but they are both functions of  r and u. Hence parameter splitting is not necessary for independence.)

Then, we encounter (9) and the following statement 				
"To conclude, conditional independence originates from no-sharing-parameter block and the independence of noise in reparameterization trick, which can be regarded as inductive biases on model."

Unfortunately, this conclusion is not correct. (9) is the defining property of an encoder with a factorized Gaussian -- it does not follow from 'non-sharing' of parameters. To see this, assume each mu_j = f(x), i.e. all means are the same, all parameters are shared. This is not a very flexible encoder distribution but still enjoys the same conditional independence structure, because parameter sharing and independence are different concepts. 

(8) is misleading as mu and sigma are not random variables in a VAE.

I suspect there may be some interesting ideas here but the paper clearly needs further iterations for clarification of concepts so it is accessible for the general technical audience.

content.title: Initial Response to R2
content.comment:
Thanks for your insightful comments. Most of them will help to improve the paper. 

Q1. “The paper is extremely difficult to read and it is hard to follow the reasoning of the authors”, and some notions should be clarified. 
A1. We will improve the narrative of the paper in revision and the next version. 

Q2. “How can the first sentence be claimed if there is not a consensus about the formal definition of disentangled representations as stated in the introduction?” 
A2. We claim independence is not sufficient mainly due to an intuitive motivation: disentanglement is about the relation between data and its representations due to Bengio's statement, while independence is just the inner property of representations (has nothing to do with input data). Also, Locatello’s impossibility theorem shows that with inductive biases, merely ensuring independence is not sufficient for Bengio’s statement of disentanglement (and our assumption is also not sufficient). 

Q3. The difference between our assumption with independence. 
A3. The main difference is that our assumption is about the relation between data and its disentangled representations, while independence is the inner property of representations. When factors in the latent variable is independent, our assumption can not be satisfied, and vice versa. In the paper, we further prove that these two assumptions are equivalent if and only if conditional independence is satisfied. Hence our assumption is an organic combination of independence and conditional independence with clear math foundation. 

Q4. The source of conditional independence excludes no-sharing-parameter block. 
A4. As you point out, now we realize that the factorized noise is sufficient for conditional independence using a factorized Gaussian variational family, and “no-sharing-parameter block” is not necessary. 

Fortunately this minor technical issue does not change the subsequent analysis and concusion of the paper, has thus has no influence on the proposed model and experimental results. We will correct it in the new version.

To be specific, we make this mistake due to wrongly regarding \mu|x and \sigma|x as stochastic variables. When they are stochastic variables, their independence are necessary for the conditional independence of z; when they are deterministic (i.e. their distributions are delta distributions), their independence are not necessary any more as the factorizing of p(z|x) is determined by the noise of reparameterization.

content.title: Correcting a mistake
content.comment:
Dear reviewers and readers:

We find that we make a mistake when designing an experiment to verify the effect of no-sharing-parameter block. Specifically, sharing-parameter encoder (describing in the second paragraph of section 5.1) is to remove no-sharing-parameter block and hence verify the necessity of conditional independence for disentanglement. In the current version, we replace the fully-connected layers in encoder with conv layers and name the encoder as sharing-parameter encoder, which do not remove no-sharing-parameter block because parameters in the last conv layer is not shared for different factors. 
To correct this mistake, we propose another design for sharing-parameter encoder: the last fully-connected layer in encoder is set to share bias for different factors. Experiment results still support our theory. Code of the corrected sharing-parameter encoder (conv_s_encoder in architecture.py) and experiment results (fig2_1.png for Vanilla VAE and fig2_2.png for FactorVAE) can be found in: https://github.com/website-for-iclr/our-dlib.

We apologize for our mistake and we will correct it in the final version.

content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I carefully checked the derivations and theory.
content.review:
Summary: 
The paper provides new information theoretic definitions for disentanglement under which the combination of statistical independence of factors and conditional independence are sufficient for achieving disentanglement. They then argued that existing approach do not successfully enforce conditional independence and thus propose new architecture that they claim improve the enforcement of conditional independence, and then show empirically that their methods work.

Decision:
Reject. This paper makes a number of claims that are either conceptually problematic or mathematically incorrect.

Issue 1: Conceptually problematic definitions of disentanglement

First, their definition of disentanglement is problematic as it admits models that are arguably not disentangled. The proof that their definition admits such undesirable models can be constructed exactly via Locatello’s impossibility theorem in conjunction with use of an invertible model to ensure that “for any factor z_j, its containing information in data is irrelevant to other factors”. 

For a simpler example consider the case of an invertible discrete latent variable model G: Z -> X where p(Z) is uniform. Suppose further that each dimension of Z is interpretable. Such a model satisfies the author’s information theoretic definition of disentanglement. However, if you permute the space of Z via a permutation function P, the resulting model will still satisfy the author’s information theoretic definition but fail to be interpretable. 

Issue 2: Misuse of the term conditional independence

Conditional independence of q(z|x) is strictly a consequence of the variational family of choice. The assertion that increasing the “no-sharing-parameter” block will further encourage conditional independence in q(z|x) is thus incorrect. Once you have committed to using a factorized Gaussian variational family, you are using a q(z|x) strictly satisfies conditional independence. Increasing the no-sharing-parameter block is will not “encourage” any additional independence. 

I am completely willing to accept the possibility that increasing the no-sharing-parameter block may empirically improve the recovery of interpretable features. However, attempting to justify the no-sharing-parameter block by appealing to a flawed application of information theory and misunderstanding of the variational family in VAEs hurts the legitimacy of the paper. 

I strongly recommend the authors to rethink the narrative of the paper.

content.title: Initial Response to R1
content.comment:
Thanks for your comments, and some are useful. Here we quickly give our key points to help calrify the potential misunderstanding. Neither do we provide new definitions for disentanglement, nor do we claim that independence and conditional independence are sufficient for disentanglement. We just propose a necessary but not sufficient assumption for disentanglement, which is different from independence. 

Q1. Conceptually problematic definitions of disentanglement. 
A1. To clarify, this paper does not present new definitions for disentanglement, nor claims (or implies) our assumption can break Locatello’s impossibility theorem. We just propose an intuitively necessary but not sufficient assumption for disentanglement to describe the relation between data and its disentangled representations. And we connect the proposed assumption with conditional independence and independence. 

Q2. Misuse of the term conditional independence. 
A2. In our paper, we do not claim that “no-sharing-parameter” block will further encourage conditional independence. In the paper, we “claim” that the root cause of conditional independence include both “no-sharing-parameter block” and factorized noise in encoder, and the “no-sharing-parameter” block is to prevent the zero-information case.

As you point out, now we realize that the factorized noise is sufficient for conditional independence using a factorized Gaussian variational family, and “no-sharing-parameter block” is not necessary. 

Fortunately this minor technical issue does not change the subsequent analysis and concusion of the paper, thus has no influence on the proposed model and experimental results. We will correct it in the new version.

content.title: Official Blind Review #4
content.review_assessment:_thoroughness_in_paper: I read the paper at least twice and used my best judgement in assessing the paper.
content.review:
Summary:
The paper proposes a new technique for unsupervised learning of disentangled representations. The new module is called "split encoder", and is derived by adding an information isolation requirement for each of the factors of variation. 
Different from  unsupervised techniques which enforce independence of the different factors. Here the relation between the representation and the data is discussed, revealing the importance of conditional independence of factors.  



Pros:
While a bit hard to follow at times, the writing is quite good and the topic is important and relevant to the field. 
I appreciated the theoretical derivations of this work, emphasizing the relation to data when 
discussing disentangled representations. The connection between the independent information assumption and the two KL terms is also quite interesting. 
Figure 2 and 3 nicely demonstrate the assumed correlation between MIG and the conditional independence. 


Major issues:

My main issue with this work is the split encoder contribution. I didn't find very strong evidence of significant gain due to the split module. To adopt such modifications in standard architectures like VAE's, a much more rigorous experimentation is needed show possibly multiple levels of independence and not just two (split / no-split). 

One important inductive bias is not discussed i believe, which is the number of factors. This seems assumed to be known in advance. Related to this is how can we prevent the case of combining two factors into one latent dimension? I think this will still fulfill the information requirement...,but could surely hurt generalization-ability. 

As explicitly stated in Section 2, the assumption is not sufficient to guarantee disentanglement and the reconstruction error should indicate that one does not converge to the trivial solution of zero mutual information between z and x. That said, looking at the reconstructions in Figure 5, there seem to be a pretty high error for such easy data. I certainly find it hard to agree with the description: "the learned representations are well disentangled except some small flaws". In fact, the Vanilla VAE results appear more appealing and not less disentangled to my eyes.  Also, in Figure 8 the highest MIG is for the vanilla VAE. 

In Section 5.2.2 a result for cars 3D behaves differently than dSprites. This is one reason (among many others) to show experiments on more than 2 datasets. I believe the work by Locatello et. al. speaks strongly for that and should be taken seriously. Even more so when using a single metric (MIG). Moreover, the explanation given on the strength of the enforced disentanglement, can it be verified by increasing betta for vanilla-VAE? I would be much more convinced by this explanation. 

Lastly, in the end of 5.2.2 the authors state: "o..obviously have better reconstructions...". IMO, the results are very much alike. Perhaps specific pointer or zoom-ins to better reconstructions example would be helpful, but from staring at the results for a bit, I can't say there is an obvious advantage to the split-encoder. 

Minor issues:
This one is not clear to me: ".. And rarely ensuring independence like FactorVAE is not sufficient for learning disentangled.."

the analysis in 5.2.1 about dSprites being simple, etc. is not clear to me. 

in the kl-div Vs. reconstruction error experiment, what are the different data points? also, how are the recon-errors measured? (what units is 1490-1510?)

some typos spotted:
"cannot ensures"
5.2.1: combing -> combining
"Therefore, for a single factor..." --> the variable there should be z_j and not z, i think.

content.title: Initial Response to R4
content.comment:
Thanks for your detailed and helpful comments. We would like to restate the motivation of the paper is to study the relation between disentangled representations and data, differing from the existing works focusing on disentangled representations themselves. We propose an assumption to connect disentangled representations with data via mutual information, and prove the assumption to be closely related to independence and conditional independence. Then we find inductive biases on encoder for conditional independence, and our assumption naturally inspires the development of the split encoder, which is a newly devised model in our paper.

The essence of this paper is establishing the strict information-theoretic relation between data and its disentangled representations, as well as inductive biases. In fact, the proposed split encoder model can be naturally derived from the proposed assumption.
 
We appreciate your efforts to carefully check the theory and experiment, and we address your questions as follows:

Q1. “I didn't find very strong evidence of significant gain due to the split module.”
A1. We tend to hold the opinion that some your concerned issues (Q3, Q4, Q5) are somewhat subjective thus cannot disprove the effectiveness of our split encoder. To better communicate with the reviewers, we can also simply view split encoder as an inductive bias for encouraging independence, which well coincides with all the experiment results in the paper.

Q2. “A much more rigorous experimentation is needed show possibly multiple levels of independence.”
A2. Thanks for your suggestion. We will consider to calculate the total correlation, which might show that our split encoder encourages lowering it, and hence demonstrates that our split encoder encourages independence. 

Q3. The number of factors is not discussed.
A3. We use the architectures in Locatello’s disentanglement lib (https://github.com/google-research/disentanglement_lib), in which the number of factors is simply set to be 10. We also set the number of factors on Cars3D as 20, but the experiment results make no difference. Therefore, we believe that setting the number of factors as 10 is sufficient for dSprite and Cars3D. We will demonstrate the number setting in the next version. 

Q4. “Looking at the reconstructions in Figure 5, there seem to be a pretty high error for such easy data”, and performance of reconstructions on images seems similar in Figure 8?
A4. The low quality of reconstructed images might be a drawback of the simple VAE architecture we utilized (which is from disentanglement lib), and cannot prove our split encoder unable to improve reconstructions. Although our split encoder cannot apparently improve reconstructed images quality on dSprite, but the reconstructed images on Cars3D using split encoder are sharper and contain more details (the raw images will be added in next version). In fact, we think the quality of image reconstruction can be subjective, especially for subtle difference under limited resolution. While the reconstruction error in the VAE’s objective can be more direct and quantitative which is popular in literature. Our split encoder obtains lower reconstruction error than all baselines on different datasets.

Q5. In Figure 5, “the Vanilla VAE（traversals）results appear more appealing and not less disentangled”.
A5. We agree that the traversals of vanilla VAE with split encoder in the paper are not perfect: the position of objective can flash from one end to another. We believe that disentanglement is a global property of representations, and may not be able to fully avoid such a subtle artifacts. In fact, our model outpeforms vanilla VAE clearly by the standard MIG score. Moreover, the subtle artifacts on one single image sample by nake eyes cannot statistically disprove the effectiveness of our method. 

Q6. “In Figure 8 the highest MIG is for the vanilla VAE.”
A6. This is normal that sometimes the result by a previous model can be better than ours on a very specific point, but we have shown that overall the results in statistics (mean or median) are better. This is why we choose violin plot to show our results. Thank you that your concern also calls our attention to the comparison of vanilla VAE’s and FactorVAE’s results on Cars3D. We carefully check the results and find that FactorVAE does not improve MIG on Cars3D (this may imply that the attributes in Cars3D is not well disentangled), but our split encoder improves the performance of FactorVAE and outperforms vanilla VAE. This indeed verifies the strength of our split encoder.

Q7. Experiments on more than 2 datasets are needed and verify the strength of split encoder by increasing beta for vanilla VAE.
A7. These advice are helpful, we will consider them in the next version.
